nodes.label: Perfect completeness
nodes.statement: For completeness, a proper colouring, its low-degree extension, exact vanishing certificates and honest lines tables, with degrees below $b^c$, pass every check for every seed: one fixed eight-table proof with perfect completeness.

nodes.label: Repetition on the same proof
nodes.locator: Repetition on the same proof, Section 7
nodes.statement: After fair-bit sampling the rejection gap is at least $g_c/16$, and constantly many independent repetitions on the same proof reduce soundness error to $1/2$, keeping logarithmic randomness and constant queries.
nodes.boundary: A result as the authors number it. Its links to the Lean were made with AI for Proof Reader and have not been reviewed by the authors.

nodes.label: The reverse inclusion
nodes.statement: For the converse, take the verifier and bounds $p,\alpha,\beta$ of Theorem 1.1, guess the first $p(n)$ proof bits and simulate the verifier, in polynomial time, on each of the at most $2^\beta(2(n+2))^\alpha$ random strings. Perfect completeness gives a prefix accepted on every run. If such a prefix existed for a no-instance, its zero extension would have acceptance probability one, contradicting soundness. The resulting witness relation is decidable in polynomial time, so the language lies in NP.
nodes.boundary: A result as the authors number it. Its links to the Lean were made with AI for Proof Reader and have not been reviewed by the authors.

nodes.label: Lemma 5.2
nodes.statement: **Lemma 5.2 (zero-on-grid test; cf. [ABSSW26, Theorem 6.1]).** The zero-on-grid test checks (2) on tables of $A$ and a certificate. It samples uniform $x,L$, reads the bit $a_{\rm bit}$ of $A$'s table at $(x,L)$ and, with the same $x,L$ and independent seeds, gets $b_0,b_Z$ or rejection from the certificate's local corrector at $(x,0)$ and $(x,Z_H(x))$; it accepts exactly when neither rejects, $b_0=0$ and $b_Z=a_{\rm bit}$. Under the hypotheses of Theorem 5.1, let $A$ and a proposed certificate $M$ have degree at most $D$, with tables at homogeneous distances $\delta_A,\delta_M$ from their encodings. If $A$ does not vanish on $H^k$ and the test rejects with probability $\kappa$, then (15) holds.
